doc.title: Houston Person Part 2 interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 2, 1998 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Advice to come to New York
summary: Person advises young musicians to spend time in New York and recalls old advice to wear a dark suit, be on time and know the blues, 'Stardust' and 'Body and Soul'.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Oh boy. What’s the New York City scene like for musicians like yourself these days. Is it worth making the effort to try to play in the city?

Well I don’t think city. I think universal. You’ve got to figure out where you want to make your home. Now I advise all young musicians or any musician, they have to come to New York, at least for a while. Because that’s where the best is. And then you can go wherever you want to live. A lot of guys live a lot of different places, but they have been to New York and played with the best and got the experience of hard knocks, and then settle down and make a living. And you can make a living in the city playing music. I always tell guys you know, and an old musician told me once, you know because somebody always gives you advice, you know you say, “get a dark suit, a white shirt, a dark tie, be on time, learn the blues, ‘Stardust” and ‘Body and Soul’ and you’ll work.” And I did that. And I worked. But basically music is so many fingers on it, so many ways you can make a living in it. But it’s good to come to New York when you’re young, and before you get a family and decide what you want to do. There’s so many ways. I love music because there is — I don’t think there’s too many fields where you can be so many different things. I mean a promoter, producer, engineer, you know so many different things.
